steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a Fog-as-a-Service framework for deploying services in public (volunteer) Fog environments with autoscaling. Explain the scaling problem, what existing Fog frameworks and autoscaling approaches miss, our aim and contributions, and how the paper is organised.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Fog computing in public settings and the need to scale
2. Estimating how many devices to scale: under- vs over-provisioning
3. Existing Fog frameworks and platforms
4. Autoscaling with orchestration tools and its limits
5. Aim and contributions
6. Paper organisation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Fog computing
- latest paradigm; computation closer to end devices; Cloud-like services for smarter applications
- public setting: anyone can provide devices to process user requests
- infrastructure not fully dedicated, no centralised control
- number of users growing and will keep rising -> longer time to serve requests -> need to scale up resources by deploying services

2. Scaling problem
- volunteer environment, sudden load spikes -> find exact number of suitable devices to scale/descale virtual Fog devices
- goal: ensure QoS, maximise resource utilisation
- estimate too low -> under-provisioning, load on devices up, QoS may fail
- estimate too high -> over-provisioning; scarce resources -> more rejections, higher cost
- complex: uncertain behaviour, high dynamics of resource changes, high mobility of Fog devices
- many end-users subscribe -> load can spike any time

3. Existing frameworks
- few Fog frameworks/platforms/services to manage devices and orchestrate workload
- Santoro et al.: Foggy, workload orchestration framework + platform
- Powell et al.: Fog Development Kit (FDK), abstracts resource allocation, high-level interfaces for rapid development; autoscaling left as future work

4. Orchestration tools
- Fog systems built on existing container orchestration + analytical tools; default autoscaling of the tools
- default schemes scale on currently available resources; ignore that resources not fully dedicated
- alone, no QoS guarantee in volunteer Fog

5. Aim + contributions
- Fog as a service: effective, autoscaling IoT services in Fog environment
- on-demand virtual Fog resources for IoT and other services, even under sudden load spikes
- (1) propose + implement FaaS for efficient deployment in public Fog
- (2) autoscaling: predict future workloads, dynamically estimate future device state from current state

6. Organisation
- II related work (autoscaling in Fog systems/platforms); III design objectives; IV system model + dynamic resource scaler (device minimum availability); V real-time cases; VI experiment results; VII conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Fog computing is the latest computing paradigm, and it brings computation power closer to the end devices so that services like the Cloud can be provided for a wide range of smarter applications. In a public setting anyone can take part in the Fog computing environment by giving devices that process the service requests of the users. This infrastructure is not fully dedicated to providing services and it has no centralised control. The number of users who request the services is often growing and will keep rising, and this increases the time to serve requests, so Fog systems need to scale up the resources by deploying the services.

To deploy and manage services in this volunteer environment and handle the sudden load spikes efficiently, we need to find the exact number of suitable devices for scaling and descaling the virtual Fog devices. This way the Quality of Service (QoS) is ensured and the overall resource utilisation is maximised. If the system estimates too low a number of devices to scale, there will be under-provisioning. Then the load on the devices increases and the QoS of the applications might not be met. If the system estimates too high a number, there will be over-provisioning. Because resources are scarce, the number of rejected service requests can be high and the cost goes up. So this is a complex task, because of the uncertain behaviour, the high dynamics of resource changes and the high mobility of Fog devices in Fog computing environments. Also, since a large number of end-users subscribe to the services, the application load can spike at any time.

There are a few Fog frameworks, platforms and services for managing Fog devices and orchestrating the application workload. Santoro et al. proposed Foggy, which is an architectural framework and platform for workload orchestration. Powell et al. proposed the Fog Development Kit (FDK), which abstracts the complexities of resource allocation and gives developers high-level interfaces so they can develop systems quickly. But the authors left the autoscaling feature for future work.

4. Orchestration tools
- Fog systems built on existing container orchestration + analytical tools; default autoscaling of the tools
- default schemes scale on currently available resources; ignore that resources not fully dedicated
- alone, no QoS guarantee in volunteer Fog

5. Aim + contributions
- Fog as a service: effective, autoscaling IoT services in Fog environment
- on-demand virtual Fog resources for IoT and other services, even under sudden load spikes
- (1) propose + implement FaaS for efficient deployment in public Fog
- (2) autoscaling: predict future workloads, dynamically estimate future device state from current state

6. Organisation
- II related work (autoscaling in Fog systems/platforms); III design objectives; IV system model + dynamic resource scaler (device minimum availability); V real-time cases; VI experiment results; VII conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Fog computing is the latest computing paradigm, and it brings computation power closer to the end devices so that services like the Cloud can be provided for a wide range of smarter applications. In a public setting anyone can take part in the Fog computing environment by giving devices that process the service requests of the users. This infrastructure is not fully dedicated to providing services and it has no centralised control. The number of users who request the services is often growing and will keep rising, and this increases the time to serve requests, so Fog systems need to scale up the resources by deploying the services.

To deploy and manage services in this volunteer environment and handle the sudden load spikes efficiently, we need to find the exact number of suitable devices for scaling and descaling the virtual Fog devices. This way the Quality of Service (QoS) is ensured and the overall resource utilisation is maximised. If the system estimates too low a number of devices to scale, there will be under-provisioning. Then the load on the devices increases and the QoS of the applications might not be met. If the system estimates too high a number, there will be over-provisioning. Because resources are scarce, the number of rejected service requests can be high and the cost goes up. So this is a complex task, because of the uncertain behaviour, the high dynamics of resource changes and the high mobility of Fog devices in Fog computing environments. Also, since a large number of end-users subscribe to the services, the application load can spike at any time.

There are a few Fog frameworks, platforms and services for managing Fog devices and orchestrating the application workload. Santoro et al. proposed Foggy, which is an architectural framework and platform for workload orchestration. Powell et al. proposed the Fog Development Kit (FDK), which abstracts the complexities of resource allocation and gives developers high-level interfaces so they can develop systems quickly. But the authors left the autoscaling feature for future work.

Some researchers have built Fog systems with existing container orchestration and analytical tools, and these give autoscaling features by using the default autoscaling scheme, technique or feature of the orchestration tools. But in these default schemes the resources are scaled based on the resources that are currently available. So these schemes ignored the fact that the resources are not fully dedicated to providing services. This means that just adopting these schemes or techniques in a volunteer Fog infrastructure does not guarantee the QoS of the services.

So the aim of this work is to develop the Fog as a service that can deliver effective and autoscaling IoT services in a Fog environment. The main idea is a framework that can provide on-demand virtual Fog resources efficiently for IoT and other services, even when there are sudden load spikes.

The contributions of this paper are:

- 1. We propose and implement a FaaS to deploy services efficiently in public Fog environments.

- 2. An autoscaling technique that predicts future workloads and dynamically estimates the future state of the Fog devices from their current state.

The paper is organised like this. Section II discusses related works on autoscaling in Fog computing systems and platforms. Section III describes the design objectives of the Fog as a Service. Section IV gives an overview of the system model and discusses the dynamic resource scaler algorithm that uses device minimum availability information. Section V gives detailed information about real-time cases. Section VI presents the results of the experiments in different scenarios. Section VII concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Fog computing is the latest computing paradigm, bringing computation power closer to the end devices to provide Cloud-like services for a wide range of smarter applications [1,2,3,4]. In public settings, anyone can participate in the Fog computing environment by providing devices to process the service requests of users. This infrastructure is not fully dedicated to providing services and there is no centralised control. Fog systems are required to scale up resources by deploying services, since the number of users requesting the services is often growing and will continue to rise, which increases the time to serve requests.

Deploying and managing services in this volunteer environment so as to efficiently handle sudden load spikes requires finding the exact number of suitable devices to scale and descale the virtual Fog devices. In this way, Quality of Service (QoS) is ensured while overall resource utilisation is maximised. If the system estimates the number of devices to scale too low, this leads to under-provisioning: the load on the devices increases and the QoS of the applications may not be met. If the system estimates the number too high, this leads to over-provisioning; due to the scarcity of resources, the number of rejected service requests may be high and the cost increases. Hence, this is a complex task, due to the uncertain behaviour, the high dynamics of resource changes and the high mobility of Fog devices in Fog computing environments. Moreover, because services are subscribed to by a large number of end-users, the application load can spike at any point in time.

A few Fog frameworks, platforms and services exist to manage Fog devices and orchestrate the application workload. Santoro et al. [5] proposed a workload orchestration architectural framework and platform called Foggy. Powell et al. [6] proposed a Fog Development Kit (FDK) that abstracts the complexities of resource allocation and provides high-level interfaces for developers to rapidly develop systems. However, the authors left the autoscaling feature as future work.

A number of researchers have built Fog systems using existing container orchestration and analytical tools, providing autoscaling features by exploiting the default autoscaling scheme, technique or feature of the orchestration tools [7,8,9,10]. However, in these default schemes the resources are scaled based on the currently available resources, ignoring the fact that the resources are not fully dedicated to providing services. Thus, adopting these schemes or techniques alone in a volunteer Fog infrastructure does not guarantee the Quality of Service (QoS) of services.

This work therefore aims to develop the Fog as a service that can deliver effective and autoscaling IoT services in a Fog environment. The main idea is to develop a framework that can efficiently provide on-demand virtual Fog resources for IoT and other services, even under sudden load spikes.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

- 1. We propose and implement a FaaS to efficiently deploy services in public Fog environments.

- 2. An autoscaling technique based on predicting future workloads and dynamically estimating the future state of the Fog devices from their current state.

The paper is organised as follows. Section II discusses related works on autoscaling in Fog computing systems and platforms. Section III describes the design objectives of the Fog as a Service. Section IV gives an overview of the system model and discusses the dynamic resource scaler algorithm that exploits device minimum availability information. Section V provides detailed information about real-time cases. Section VI presents the results of experiments obtained in different scenarios. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper.

References:

[2] K. Ujjwal, S. Garg, J. Hilton, and J. Aryal, “A cloud-based framework for sensitivity analysis of natural hazard models,” Environmental Modelling & Software , vol. 134, p. 104800, 2020.

[5] D. Santoro, D. Zozin, D. Pizzolli, F. De Pellegrini, and S. Cretti, “Foggy: A platform for workload orchestration in a fog computing environment,” in 2017 IEEE International Conference on Cloud Computing Technology and Science (CloudCom) . IEEE, 2017, pp. 231–234.
[6] C. Powell, C. Desiniotis, and B. Dezfouli, “The fog development kit: A platform for the development and management of fog systems,” IEEE Internet of Things Journal , vol. 7, no. 4, pp. 3198–3213, 2020.
